extracted.intended_audience: patent and trademark practitioners (attorneys, in-house counsel, agents) handling prosecution and litigation in Colombia (Andean Community) and nearby jurisdictions
extracted.subtask_description: Practical rules, procedural requirements, and substantive enforcement standards for prosecuting, defending, and litigating patents and trademarks in Colombia (including references to Andean Decision 486 and related CPO/CTO practice). Covers oppositions, examination, amendments, infringement, invalidity, remedies, evidence, and costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition filing window (patents)
rubrics_metrics.description: May file an opposition within 60 days following the publication of the application (extendable for the same term upon request).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The CPO must consider the arguments and evidence provided in an opposition during examination. There is no separate or independent opposition procedure, and thus oppositions do not introduce delay in prosecution exceeding 2-3 months. Third parties may also file observations at any time before final decision, but it is optional for the Office to consider these arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner interviews (patents)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiner interviews are allowed and are easy to obtain (by simply requesting a meeting at the CPO Office).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interviews are highly recommended, as they are useful in a good number of cases to facilitate prosecution and grant; interviewing examiners to discuss options can materially affect prosecution speed and outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent term and term extensions
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent term is 20 years from the filing or from the international filing date in the case of PCT National Phase applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under Decree 1873 of 2014, term extensions are available as compensation for “unreasonable” delays if prosecution lasted more than 5 years from filing date or 3 years from the examination request date. Pharmaceuticals are expressly excluded from extensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expedited examination / PPH
rubrics_metrics.description: No laws providing accelerated examination; diligent prosecution may reduce terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Request examination as soon as the application is published. Patent Prosecution Highway (PPH) programs are available and Colombia has PPH agreements with multiple offices (EPO, Japan, Korea, Spain, US and Pacific Alliance partners). PPHs are an option to speed examination, subject to each PPH's regulations and implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim amendments during prosecution
rubrics_metrics.description: Voluntary claim amendments are possible at any time during prosecution and, in any case, before a final decision granting the patent is issued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amendments cannot extend the original scope of the invention and must find support in the specification. If the patent is rejected, claims can be further amended by filing a Reconsideration Action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divisional application practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Divisionals may be filed at any time during prosecution, even after a non-final rejection; parent claim sets must explicitly carve out the divisional application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims in parent and divisional can be amended after filing as necessary. The Specification of the divisional should be adapted to reflect to some degree the particular subject-matter that was divided (e.g., remove subject-matter of the divisional from the parent's Specification). Under Resolution 3719, divisionals from divisionals are not allowed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional applications (Andean)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provisional applications are not available under Andean Decision 486.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of exclusionary rights (patent infringement)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the patent protects a product, the patent owner can prevent third parties from importing, using, manufacturing, offering for sale or selling the product without consent. For method patents, the owner can prevent third parties from using the method or performing acts involving products obtained directly through the protected method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A patent will be infringed if any of its claims read on an allegedly infringing product or process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literal infringement standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Only literal infringement is contemplated under Andean Decision 486.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The doctrine of equivalents has not been recognized in Colombia, although judges are prone to give expansive interpretations of key elements when they feel it is equitable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of infringement and inducement
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct infringement is explicitly recognized; indirect (inducement or contributory infringement) is not specifically contemplated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article 238 of Decision 486 allows enforcement against individuals who execute acts that present imminence of infringement; under a broad interpretation, inducement presenting high risk of infringement may be actionable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural options and primary venues (patent enforcement)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent holder may pursue civil or criminal action to stop or prevent infringement acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Civil actions may be filed before civil court judges or before the CPO's Judicial Division (JD). Colombia is implementing an expedited oral procedure; CPO JD has become a principal and effective venue. Typical civil patent litigation stages include: preliminary injunction request (ex parte), complaint filing, admission/service, defendant's reply, conciliation hearing/evidence gathering/oral closings, mandatory prejudicial interpretation before the Andean Court of Justice where applicable, and final ruling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal standing for patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Legal standing is limited to the titleholder; if multiple titleholders exist, any of them may sue independently unless otherwise agreed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Declaratory judgments are very rare but a potential infringer may request declaration that its conduct does not infringe the patent rights if the patent holder has not yet filed suit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bifurcated system and invalidity procedure (patents)
rubrics_metrics.description: Colombia has a bifurcated system: invalidity cannot be used as a defense within an infringement lawsuit; a separate lawsuit is required to invalidate the patent (Annulment Action against the CPO before the Council of State).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The purpose of an annulment action is to show the granting resolution violated the Constitution, Decision 486 or any procedural/substantive law. Burden of proof is carried by the party seeking to invalidate the patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judges' level of IP expertise by forum
rubrics_metrics.description: Judges’ level of IP expertise is graded from 1 to 3 (3 highest) across forums (Civil Courts, Criminal Courts, CPO Judicial Division, Attorney General’s Office, Contentious Administrative First Section/Council of State).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The guide provides a scored table indicating relative expertise in different fora (useful to choose venue strategically).

rubrics_metrics.name: Litigation delay estimates (patents)
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimated timelines: first instance before CPO ~5-12 months; second instance ~2 years on average; a patent infringement case litigated before CPO and in second instance could take ~3 years to final decision (2014 data). Preliminary injunctions can be obtained between 6 to 15 days; preliminary injunctions via CPO may be quicker (6–15 days).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delays vary by complexity and venue; these are empirical CPO-published estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statute of limitations for patent claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 244 of Decision 486: time limit to seek a remedy is 2 years from the date the patent holder had knowledge of the infringement or, in any case, 5 years from the date the last act of infringement occurred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For calculating the date, CPO JD does not consider acts of infringement to be continuing and uses the first date of infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary injunctions and ex-parte relief
rubrics_metrics.description: Preliminary injunctions (ex parte) are the most efficient way to stop infringement; injunctive relief can include seizure of goods, suspension of importation, or establishment of a bond.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preliminary injunctions are reviewed/granted without defendant participation; plaintiffs need only show good title and evidence of infringement (often via expert affidavit). Bonds must be posted (see bond rubric); judge may suspend injunction based on necessity, reasonability, proportionality. Defendant may request revocation via reconsideration and can suspend injunction effects by posting a counter-bond.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bonds for injunctions
rubrics_metrics.description: A bond must be offered and posted to cover potential damages caused by the injunction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under Colombian procedure law, it is necessary to post a bond equivalent to 20% of the estimated total value of the claims requested by the plaintiff. A counter-bond by defendant can suspend injunction effects while appeal is pending.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert evidence importance
rubrics_metrics.description: Expert evidence is critical in any patent suit (infringement or invalidity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties may submit own experts and the court may appoint its own; multiple experts are typical. Expert affidavits often used to establish infringement; in invalidity trials experts help interpret technical issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery and pre-trial procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Colombian law provides mechanisms enabling pre-trial discovery and other pre-trial procedures, including preliminary injunctions to preserve evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discovery requests include site inspections, document productions, depositions, witness testimonies, and expert opinions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary support admissibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Colombian law does not place limits on types of evidence admissible in civil procedure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common evidence: witness testimony, expert opinions provided by parties, court-ordered expert opinions, site inspections, documents (including electronic) and requests for production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof (patents)
rubrics_metrics.description: Burden of proof normally lies on the plaintiff in infringement actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For method claims, burden can be reversed onto the defendant who must demonstrate the infringing method is different from the patented one. For invalidity trials, the burden is on the party seeking to invalidate the patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages calculation alternatives (patents and trademarks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 243 of Decision 486 provides alternatives to calculate compensation: (i) lost profits and actual damages, (ii) unjust enrichment, and (iii) reasonable royalty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Punitive damages are not provided for in Colombian legislation. Damages claim period can include the time between the date the patent/trademark became public and the granting date. Very few cases get to damages stage because preliminary injunctions are often sufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Average lawsuit costs (patents)
rubrics_metrics.description: Costs vary by complexity. For infringement cases, reasonable budgets across litigation lifespan (estimated two-to-four years) range between USD 75,000 and USD 250,000. For invalidity suits, costs on average can range between USD 100,000 and USD 250,000.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Costs depend on complexity and type of evidence used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appellate practice and standards of review
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties may appeal adverse trial court decisions to superior courts; infringement cases may eventually be selected to be heard by the Supreme Court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invalidity suits are single-instance procedures with no appeals available. The standard of review for appeals is de novo, although deference is normally given to findings of fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Settlement and alternative dispute resolution (patents)
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties may voluntarily settle infringement cases at their convenience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For invalidity cases, settlement/ADR are not available because the defendant is the CPO; however, parties may agree to arbitration and can include alternatives to incorporate invalidity issues in contractual dispute-resolution clauses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fee shifting (patents and trademarks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Attorney fees as set by the national bar are available for winning parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The successful litigant may recover these attorney fees by requesting the judge to order the losing party to pay; in practice the amount set by the bar and recognized by the judge may not correspond to the true invoiced fees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal liability (criminal infringement)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is personal liability for a conviction in criminal infringement actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criminal infringements are rare; Attorney General’s Office pursues criminal IP cases, which are oral and accusatory and decided by Criminal Courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antitrust considerations when enforcing patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent rights are not absolute and are limited to the scope of the claims as granted; unduly broad interpretation could be interpreted as abuse of IP rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a patent holder has a dominant market position, sham litigation based on patents could be taken as an abuse of dominant position. There is limited judicial/antitrust authority precedent in Colombia on this point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of trademarks (registrable signs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Per Article 134 of Decision 486, registrable signs include words or combinations, pictures/figures/symbols/graphic elements, labels, logotypes, monograms, portraits, emblems, sounds and smells, letters and numbers, color with borders to generate a specific shape, shape of a product/packaging/form, and combinations thereof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decision 486 allows registration of non-traditional trademarks (sounds, smells, textures), but the CTO applies a very high standard to grant such marks. CTO has recently recognized tactile trademarks in limited cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinctiveness and confusing similarity criteria (trademarks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Trademarks must have sufficient level of distinction versus other signs; distinctiveness is evaluated according to ideological, phonetic and visual elements, considering the class and prior coexistence in the market.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-famous trademarks mainly compared on ideological/phonetic/visual considerations. Confusing similarity analysis considers these elements alongside class and market coexistence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trademark application formalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Application formalities include: request; reproduction of the mark (word mark with graphic elements, shape or color, or figurative/mixed/three-dimensional mark with or without color); classification(s) covered by the application; power of attorney; proof of payment of prescribed fee; required authorizations under Articles 135 and 136 where applicable; and, if applicable, certificate of registration in country of origin and proof of payment for Paris Convention rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trademark registration delay typically 6–9 months; if opposed delay up to 18 months; appeal can extend another six months. Costs average about US$750 for a typical registration but increase if oppositions are filed and evidence analysis is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unregistrable marks (absolute and relative prohibitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unregistrable marks are set out in Articles 135, 136 and 137 of Decision 486 and are categorized as absolute prohibitions (inherent lack of distinctiveness, misleading signs) and relative prohibitions (likelihood of confusion with previously registered/applied marks, trade names, copyrighted material, geographical indications, well-known signs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical absolute grounds include generic, descriptive, deceiving, commonly used signs or lack of inherent/extrinsic distinctiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Famous and well-known mark protection and evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: For a famous trademark to be protected it must be well-known in Colombia or any country of the Andean Community; famous marks are protected irrespective of registration (Articles 225 and 231 of Decision 486).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrating well-known status is complex and in administrative proceedings evidence must be documentary. Ideal evidence: top-of-mind and marketing research studies, client certificates, accounting evidence, proof of advertising amount and scope. Evidence must refer specifically to the trademark and the relevant period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior user rights (trademark)
rubrics_metrics.description: The titleholder of the trademark cannot pursue an action against a third party that had been using the trademark in good faith prior to the trademark application date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographical indications and denominations of origin
rubrics_metrics.description: Geographic indications are protectable; denominations of origin can be registered according to Articles 201–223 of Decision 486.

rubrics_metrics.name: SME and special filing benefits (trademarks)
rubrics_metrics.description: The CTO Circular Única provides discounts of 25% on trademark registrations requested by natural persons without financial means, small and medium entities, recognized universities and research/ development foundations, provided they complete an industrial property course offered by the CTO and accredit attendance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition system (trademarks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Colombia provides a pre-grant opposition system: a third party may file an opposition within 30 working days following publication of the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grounds may be absolute or relative prohibitions (e.g., lack of inherent/extrinsic distinctiveness, confusing similarity). Once opposition is filed a formal study is made; if accepted for prosecution the applicant has 30 working days to file a reply, which can include evidence. The CTO will issue a final decision on the merits, including analysis of opposition grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner interviews (trademarks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiner interviews are allowed and easy to obtain (by requesting a meeting at the CTO Office).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interviews are highly recommended and can be persuasive for obtaining a trademark and facilitating prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection from pending trademark applications
rubrics_metrics.description: A pending trademark application in priority provides protection regarding other similar or equal trademarks that could be registered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unregistered trademarks may still be defended using unfair competition arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domain name registration rules (Colombia)
rubrics_metrics.description: Domain name registration in Colombia follows Resolution 1455 of 2003 and ICANN rules; .CO Internet S.A.S. handles registrations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Right of use is awarded to the first applicant; validity may not exceed two years and is renewable within the last month of validity. Cancellation can occur for technical/service reasons, non-payment of fees, or orders by authorities. Disputes handled by UDRP. Domain name registration grants exclusive use but does not transfer property rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trademark infringement remedies and stages
rubrics_metrics.description: Trademark registration provides exclusive right to use and prevent use of similar marks; infringement occurs when a non-authorized party uses an equal or similar registered mark in connection with goods/services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Types and procedural options mirror patent practice: civil or criminal actions, civil venue before civil courts or CTO JD, expedited oral procedure in development. Typical civil stages include preliminary injunction (ex parte), complaint filing, admission/service, reply, conciliation/hearing/evidence/oral closings, prejudicial interpretation before Andean Court of Justice where applicable, and final ruling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standing for trademark invalidity
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 172 of Decision 486: any person can seek the invalidity of a trademark; no additional requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Colombia uses a bifurcated system: invalidity cannot be used as a defense in infringement; a separate Annulment Action against the CTO before the Council of State is required. The purpose is to show the registration was issued in violation of applicable law or procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary and expert considerations in trademark cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Colombian law admits broad types of evidence; expert evidence is critical in trademark suits, particularly for interpreting surveys and market perception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In invalidity lawsuits experts interpreting surveys are relevant to controvert the CTO's position. Parties may submit experts and courts may appoint experts; multiple experts typical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages and remedies (trademark)
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 243 applies to trademarks as to patents: alternatives include lost profits/actual damages, unjust enrichment, and reasonable royalty; punitive damages not provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Very few trademark cases reach damages stage because preliminary injunctions are often sufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Average lawsuit costs (trademark)
rubrics_metrics.description: Costs vary by complexity and are generally invoiced hourly. Reasonable budgets for trademark lawsuits range between USD 15,000 and USD 60,000 for a 4-year period, including appeals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a preliminary injunction is successful the amount could be reduced to around USD 10,000 or less spread over a year.
